source.part: Discussion of the doctrine of equivalents
source.excerpt: While both compounds have the effect of neutralizing parasites in animals, identity of result does not amount to infringement of patent unless Albendazole operates in substantially the same way or by substantially the same means as the patented compound, even though it performs the same function and achieves the same result. In other words, the principle or mode of operation must be the same or substantially the same.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: After a court's injunction stopped its sales, a company claims lost profits as actual damages. It proves the amount only through its President and Executive Vice-President, who testify that monthly sales had been P100,000 and fell to zero. According to Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals, how should the claim be treated?

choices.A: It should be granted in full, because lost profits are always presumed after an injunction.
choices.B: It should be granted, because officers of a company are the best witnesses of its sales.
choices.C: It should be denied as actual damages, because the officers' testimony is not competent proof or the best evidence obtainable; documentary evidence is also required, though temperate damages may be awarded for a pecuniary loss that cannot be proved with certainty.
choices.D: It should be denied, and no damages of any kind may be awarded.

questions.explanation: C is correct. Actual or compensatory damages cover not only the loss suffered but also profits the injured party failed to obtain, but the actual amount must be proved with a reasonable degree of certainty, based on competent proof and the best evidence obtainable. The officers' testimonies were not the competent proof or best evidence, because such damages also require documentary evidence. The Court therefore deleted the P330,000 actual damages. It instead awarded P20,000 as temperate or moderate damages, because the company had suffered some pecuniary loss the amount of which could not, from the nature of the case, be established with certainty. A and B are wrong because the amount of damages is not presumed or established by officers' say-so alone. D is wrong because the Court did award temperate damages.

source.caseTitle: Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals and Tryco Pharma Corp.
source.part: Discussion of the awards of actual and temperate damages
source.excerpt: While indemnification for actual or compensatory damages covers not only the loss suffered (damnum emergens) but also profits which the obligee failed to obtain (lucrum cessans or ganacias frustradas), it is necessary to prove the actual amount of damages with a reasonable degree of certainty based on competent proof and on the best evidence obtainable by the injured party. The testimonies of private respondent’s officers are not the competent proof or best evidence obtainable to establish its right to actual or compensatory damages for such damages also require presentation of documentary evidence to substantiate a claim therefor. … This Court, however, grants private respondent temperate or moderate damages in the amount of ₱20,000.00 which it finds reasonable under the circumstances, it having suffered some pecuniary loss the amount of which cannot, from the nature of the case, be established with certainty.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A company is sued for patent infringement and wins. It asks for attorney's fees, arguing that it was forced to litigate to protect its rights, but there is no evidence that the patent holder acted with malice. According to Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals, should attorney's fees be awarded?

choices.A: Yes, because being forced to litigate always entitles a winning party to attorney's fees.
choices.B: No, because even if a party is compelled to litigate to protect its rights, attorney's fees may not be awarded without sufficient showing of bad faith, and persistence in a case out of an erroneous conviction of the righteousness of one's cause is not bad faith.
choices.C: Yes, because the patent holder lost the case.
choices.D: Yes, because attorney's fees are automatically awarded in every patent case.

questions.explanation: B is correct. The Court deleted the attorney's fees that the Court of Appeals had granted under Article 2208 (2) of the Civil Code. Even if a claimant is compelled to litigate with third persons or to incur expenses to protect its rights, attorney's fees may not be awarded where no sufficient showing of bad faith is reflected in a party's persistence in a case other than an erroneous conviction of the righteousness of his cause, and there was no evidence that the patent holder was moved by malice. A is wrong because being forced to litigate is not enough by itself. C is wrong because losing a case is not bad faith. D is wrong because nothing in the decision makes attorney's fees automatic.

source.caseTitle: Smith Kline Beckman Corp. v. Court of Appeals and Tryco Pharma Corp.
source.part: Discussion of the award of attorney's fees
source.excerpt: Even if a claimant is compelled to litigate with third persons or to incur expenses to protect its rights, still attorney’s fees may not be awarded where no sufficient showing of bad faith could be reflected in a party’s persistence in a case other than an erroneous conviction of the righteousness of his cause. There exists no evidence on record indicating that petitioner was moved by malice in suing private respondent.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A patent claims a hand tractor with a list of specific parts: a circular floating housing, a front wheel, a protective water covering, a transmission box, a V-shaped inclined handle and an engine base on top of the housing. The patent holder sues a shop owner whose hand tractors, when placed side by side with the patented one and photographed from every angle, have the same parts in the same arrangement and, as the shop owner admits, operate on the same principles. How should a court decide whether there is infringement under the first test of infringement, and what is the likely result? Explain, based on Godines v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The court applies the test of literal infringement. It looks first to the words of the claims and compares them with the accused product. Because the shop owner's tractors have all the material elements of the claims, the likely result is a finding of infringement.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: The tests of infringement are (a) literal infringement and (b) the doctrine of equivalents. In literal infringement, resort must be had, in the first instance, to the words of the claim, and if the accused matter clearly falls within the claim, infringement is made out and that is the end of it. To decide this, the court must juxtapose the claims of the patent and the accused product within the overall context of the claims and specifications to see whether there is exact identity of all material elements.
suggestedAnswer.application: The court compares the listed parts of the claim with the shop owner's tractors, element by element, and may inspect samples placed alongside the patented one. Here the form, configuration, design and appearance are the same, the parts are virtually the same, and the shop owner himself admits that the two operate on the same principles. The claims and the features of the patented model were evidently copied, so the accused product falls within the claims.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: There is literal infringement, and the shop owner is liable to the patent holder.

keyPoints: Two tests of infringement: literal infringement and the doctrine of equivalents
In literal infringement, resort first to the words of the claim; if the accused matter clearly falls within the claim, infringement is made out
The court juxtaposes the claims and the accused product, within the context of the claims and specifications, to see whether there is exact identity of all material elements
Inspection of samples, similarity of parts and admission that they operate on the same principles support a finding of copying

source.caseTitle: Godines v. Court of Appeals and SV-Agro Enterprises, Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the tests of infringement and the trial court's comparison of the tillers
source.excerpt: Tests have been established to determine infringement. These are (a) literal infringement; and (b) the doctrine of equivalents. In using literal infringement as a test, ". . . resort must be had, in the first instance, to the words of the claim. If accused matter clearly falls within the claim, infringement is made out and that is the end of it." To determine whether the particular item falls within the literal meaning of the patent claims, the court must juxtapose the claims of the patent and the accused product within the overall context of the claims and specifications, to determine whether there is exact identity of all material elements. … Viewed from any perspective or angle, the power tiller of the defendant is identical and similar to that of the turtle power tiller of plaintiff in form, configuration, design and appearance. The parts or components thereof are virtually the same. … It appears from the foregoing observation of the trial court that these claims of the patent and the features of the patented utility model were copied by petitioner. We are compelled to arrive at no other conclusion but that there was infringement.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A shop owner copies a patented machine but changes its name, makes the housing a little rounder and moves a handle a few centimeters. When sued for infringement, he argues that his machine is different from the patented one, so there is no literal infringement. Is the argument a good defense? Explain, based on Godines v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Under the doctrine of equivalents, minor modifications do not put a copy beyond the reach of the patent. A device that does substantially the same work in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result infringes, even if it differs in name, form or shape.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Courts adopted the doctrine of equivalents because the logical fallback of a defendant is to say that his product is different. Under it, an infringement also occurs when a device appropriates a prior invention by incorporating its innovative concept and, albeit with some modification and change, performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result. The reason for the doctrine is that allowing the imitation of a patented invention that copies no literal detail would turn the protection of the patent into a hollow and useless thing and would encourage the unscrupulous copyist to make unimportant and insubstantial changes that take the copy outside the claim.
suggestedAnswer.application: The shop owner changed only the name, the roundness of the housing and the position of a handle. Those are unimportant and insubstantial changes. What matters is what the elements do, so the court asks whether the machine performs the same function in substantially the same way and reaches substantially the same result. If so, then differences in name, form or shape are immaterial.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The defense fails. The shop owner infringes the patent under the doctrine of equivalents even though there is no literal copy.

keyPoints: Doctrine of equivalents: infringement occurs when a device, with some modification, performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result
Minor modifications do not take a copy outside the patent
Reason: otherwise the patent's protection would be hollow, and unscrupulous copyists would make insubstantial changes
Similarities and differences are judged by what the elements do, not by names; differences of form or name are immaterial

source.caseTitle: Godines v. Court of Appeals and SV-Agro Enterprises, Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the doctrine of equivalents
source.excerpt: Recognizing that the logical fallback position of one in the place of defendant is to aver that his product is different from the patented one, courts have adopted the doctrine of equivalents which recognizes that minor modifications in a patented invention are sufficient to put the item beyond the scope of literal infringement. Thus, according to this doctrine, "(a)n infringement also occurs when a device appropriates a prior invention by incorporating its innovative concept and, albeit with some modification and change, performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result." The reason for the doctrine of equivalents is that to permit the imitation of a patented invention which does not copy any literal detail would be to convert the protection of the patent grant into a hollow and useless thing. Such imitation would leave room for — indeed encourage — the unscrupulous copyist to make unimportant and insubstantial changes and substitutions in the patent which, though adding nothing, would be enough to take the copied matter outside the claim, and hence outside the reach of the law.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A machine shop owner is sued for making and selling copies of a patented machine. He says that he never made machines on his own design, but only on special order, following his customers' own specifications. The courts find that he had been making and selling similar machines long before the patent holder sold its own, that he has no job orders to show, and that it would be unusual for buyers to order such machines on verbal instructions alone. May he re-argue the point before the Supreme Court on a petition for review, and does his defense succeed? Explain, based on Godines v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No to both. Whether he made and sold the machines is a question of fact that the Supreme Court does not re-examine on a petition for review, and the courts' reasons for rejecting his defense are sound.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: The jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in a petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45 is limited to errors of law, and the findings of fact of the Court of Appeals are conclusive upon it. Whether the petitioner was manufacturing and selling the items is a question of fact better addressed to the lower courts.
suggestedAnswer.application: The trial court found the defense untenable because (1) the shop owner admitted in his Answer that he had been making and selling such machines long before the patent holder started selling its own, which showed that he was principally a manufacturer working on his own specifications and designs; (2) he showed no job orders, although it would be unbelievable for him to make copies without them, especially since he is an engineer and owns the shop; and (3) it is contrary to usual business practice, and costly and time-consuming, for buyers to order machines on verbal instructions alone. The courts therefore established that he made and sold the machines without the patentee's authority.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: He cannot re-argue the fact, and his defense fails. He made and sold the machines without authority.

keyPoints: A petition for review under Rule 45 is limited to errors of law; the findings of fact of the Court of Appeals are conclusive
Whether the accused manufactured and sold the items is a question of fact for the lower courts
No job orders were presented, and it would be unusual to make copies without specifications or to order them on verbal instructions
His admission of long-time manufacturing and selling showed that he made the machines on his own design
Making and selling without the patentee's authority was established

source.caseTitle: Godines v. Court of Appeals and SV-Agro Enterprises, Inc.
source.part: Discussion of whether petitioner manufactured and sold the tillers
source.excerpt: The question of whether petitioner was manufacturing and selling power tillers is a question of fact better addressed to the lower courts. … However, this contention appears untenable in the light of the following circumstances: 1) he admits in his Answer that he has been manufacturing power tillers or hand tractors, selling and distributing them long before plaintiff started selling its turtle power tiller in Zamboanga del Sur and Misamis Occidental, meaning that defendant is principally a manufacturer of power tillers, not upon specification and design of buyers, but upon his own specification and design; 2) it would be unbelievable that defendant would fabricate power tillers similar to the turtle power tillers of plaintiff upon specifications of buyers without requiring a job order where the specification and designs of those ordered are specified. No document was (sic) ever been presented showing such job orders, and it is rather unusual for defendant to manufacture something without the specification and designs, considering that he is an engineer by profession and proprietor of the Ozamis Engineering shop. … Of general acceptance is the rule imbedded in our jurisprudence that ". . . the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in cases brought to it from the Court of Appeals in a petition for certiorari under Rule 45 of the Rules of Court is limited to the review of errors of law, and that said appellate court's findings of fact are conclusive upon this Court." … The fact that petitioner herein manufactured and sold power tillers without patentee's authority has been established by the courts despite petitioner's claims to the contrary.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under Section 37 of Republic Act No. 165, as applied in Godines v. Court of Appeals, which act is an infringement of a patent?

choices.A: Selling an unpatented product that is similar in function to the patented one.
choices.B: Studying the patented machine in a classroom without selling anything.
choices.C: Making, using or selling the patented machine without the patentee's authorization.
choices.D: Publishing the patent in a newspaper of general circulation.

questions.explanation: C is correct. Section 37, as quoted in the decision, gives the patentee the exclusive right to make, use and sell the patented machine, article or product, and to use the patented process for the purpose of industry or commerce, throughout the Philippines for the term of the patent, and says that such making, using or selling by any person without the patentee's authorization constitutes infringement. A is wrong because a product that does not fall within the claims, literally or by equivalents, does not infringe; similarity of function alone is not the test. B is wrong because the section speaks of making, using or selling for the purpose of industry or commerce, not of studying. D is wrong because publication of the patent was something SV-Agro did, not an act of infringement. Watch for: this is the provision of the old Patent Law (Republic Act No. 165) applied in the decision; patents are now governed by the Intellectual Property Code, so check its current text.

source.caseTitle: Godines v. Court of Appeals and SV-Agro Enterprises, Inc.
source.part: Discussion of liability (Section 37 of R.A. No. 165)
source.excerpt: Sec. 37. Right of Patentees. — A patentee shall have the exclusive right to make, use and sell the patented machine, article or product, and to use the patented process for the purpose of industry or commerce, throughout the territory of the Philippines for the terms of the patent; and such making, using, or selling by any person without the authorization of the Patentee constitutes infringement of the patent.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In a patent infringement case, the defendant stresses that his machine has a different name from the patented one. According to Godines v. Court of Appeals, how are the similarities or differences between the devices determined?

choices.A: By the names the parties give to the devices, since the name identifies the invention.
choices.B: By the price and appearance of the devices as they are sold to buyers.
choices.C: By the date on which each device was first sold in the market.
choices.D: In the light of what the elements do, with substantial rather than technical identity as the test; mere differences of form or name are immaterial if the same function is performed in substantially the same way.

questions.explanation: D is correct. The decision adopts the trial court's statement that, in infringement of patent, similarities or differences are determined not by the names of things but in the light of what the elements do, and that substantial rather than technical identity is the test. It is necessary and sufficient for equivalency that the same function can be performed in substantially the same way or manner, or by the same or substantially the same principle or mode of operation, and where these tests are satisfied, mere differences of form or name are immaterial. A is the opposite of the rule. B and C are not part of the test.

source.caseTitle: Godines v. Court of Appeals and SV-Agro Enterprises, Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the doctrine of equivalents (the trial court's observation)
source.excerpt: in infringement of patent, similarities or differences are to be determined, not by the names of things, but in the light of what elements do, and substantial, rather than technical, identity in the test. More specifically, it is necessary and sufficient to constitute equivalency that the same function can be performed in substantially the same way or manner, or by the same or substantially the same, principle or mode of operation; but where these tests are satisfied, mere differences of form or name are immaterial.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A patent holder sues a competitor for infringement but cannot show that the competitor copied its device in every particular. According to Godines v. Court of Appeals, what must the patent holder show to establish infringement?

choices.A: That the defendant copied the device in every particular.
choices.B: Proof that the defendant adopted the substance of the thing is sufficient; it is not essential to show adoption in every particular.
choices.C: That the defendant's device has exactly the same mechanism described in the patent, with no difference at all.
choices.D: That the defendant acted with malice, because infringement requires bad faith.

questions.explanation: B is correct. The decision quotes the rule that to establish an infringement it is not essential to show that the defendant adopted the device or process in every particular; proof of an adoption of the substance of the thing is sufficient. A construction that limited infringement to the exact mechanism described in the patent would be so obviously unjust that no court could be expected to adopt it. A and C describe exactly that rejected approach. D is wrong because the decision does not require malice for infringement; it says that making, using or selling the patented article without authorization is infringement.

source.caseTitle: Godines v. Court of Appeals and SV-Agro Enterprises, Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the doctrine of equivalents (the trial court's quotation on substantial correspondence)
source.excerpt: To establish an infringement, it is not essential to show that the defendant adopted the device or process in every particular; Proof of an adoption of the substance of the thing will be sufficient. … The law will protect a patentee against imitation of his patent by other forms and proportions. If two devices do the same work in substantially the same way, and accomplish substantially the same result, they are the same, even though they differ in name, form, or shape.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under Section 29(a) of Republic Act No. 166, as quoted in Godines v. Court of Appeals, which person is deemed guilty of unfair competition?

choices.A: A person who sells his goods in a way that gives them the general appearance of another manufacturer's or dealer's goods, likely to influence purchasers that the goods are those of someone else, or who clothes the goods with an appearance that deceives the public and defrauds another of legitimate trade.
choices.B: A person who sells goods at a lower price than a competitor.
choices.C: A person who manufactures goods of the same kind as a competitor's without copying anything.
choices.D: A person who advertises his own goods truthfully in a newspaper.

questions.explanation: A is correct. The decision quotes Section 29(a), which says that any person who, in selling his goods, gives them the general appearance of the goods of another manufacturer or dealer, either as to the goods themselves, the wrapping, the devices or words on them, or any other feature of their appearance, which would be likely to influence purchasers that the goods are those of a different manufacturer or dealer, or who otherwise clothes the goods with an appearance that deceives the public and defrauds another of his legitimate trade, is guilty of unfair competition. B, C and D describe lawful competition and do not involve passing off. Watch for: the provision quoted is from the old Trademark Law (Republic Act No. 166), and the decision only quotes it before affirming the finding of unfair competition, so check the current law for the rule that now applies.

source.caseTitle: Godines v. Court of Appeals and SV-Agro Enterprises, Inc.
source.part: Discussion of unfair competition (Section 29 of R.A. No. 166)
source.excerpt: In particular, and without in any way limiting the scope of unfair competition, the following shall be deemed guilty of unfair competition: (a) Any person, who in selling his goods shall give them the general appearance of goods of another manufacturer or dealer, either as to the goods themselves or in the wrapping of the packages in which they are contained, or the devices or words thereon, or in any other feature of their appearance, which would be likely to influence purchasers that the goods offered are those of a manufacturer or dealer other than the actual manufacturer or dealer, or who otherwise clothes the goods with such appearance as shall deceive the public and defraud another of his legitimate trade.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A defendant found liable for patent infringement asks the Supreme Court, by petition for review under Rule 45, to review the lower courts' finding that he made and sold the patented machines. According to Godines v. Court of Appeals, what is the Supreme Court's approach?

choices.A: It re-weighs all the evidence, because patent cases are technical.
choices.B: It reviews only the trial court's findings and ignores the Court of Appeals.
choices.C: Whether he made and sold them is a question of fact; its review is limited to errors of law, and the Court of Appeals' findings of fact are conclusive upon it.
choices.D: It automatically remands the case for a new trial.

questions.explanation: C is correct. The Court said that whether the petitioner was manufacturing and selling the machines is a question of fact better addressed to the lower courts, and recalled the rule that in a Rule 45 petition its jurisdiction is limited to the review of errors of law, and the appellate court's findings of fact are conclusive upon it. A is wrong because the Court is not a trier of facts. B is wrong because the findings of the Court of Appeals are the ones treated as conclusive. D is wrong because nothing in the decision calls for a new trial; the petition was denied.

source.caseTitle: Godines v. Court of Appeals and SV-Agro Enterprises, Inc.
source.part: Discussion of whether petitioner manufactured and sold the tillers (the scope of review)
source.excerpt: The question of whether petitioner was manufacturing and selling power tillers is a question of fact better addressed to the lower courts. … Of general acceptance is the rule imbedded in our jurisprudence that ". . . the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in cases brought to it from the Court of Appeals in a petition for certiorari under Rule 45 of the Rules of Court is limited to the review of errors of law, and that said appellate court's findings of fact are conclusive upon this Court."

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A patent owner sues a competitor for infringement and obtains a restraining order. In its own complaint, the patent owner admits that its patent is valid only until a certain date. By the time an appellate court approves the bond and issues a restraining order against the competitor, that date has passed. Was the restraining order proper? Explain, based on Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The patent owner's exclusive right exists only during the term of the patent. After the patent expired, there was no right left to protect, so no restraining order or injunction could properly issue.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 37 of Republic Act No. 165, the exclusive right of the patentee to make, use and sell the patented article exists throughout the Philippines for the term of the patent, and the term was seventeen years from the date of issuance (Section 21). Under Section 4, Rule 129 of the Rules of Court, an admission made by a party in the same case does not require proof and may be contradicted only by showing palpable mistake or that no such admission was made. Two requisites must exist for injunctive relief: (1) a clear and unmistakable right that must be protected; and (2) an urgent and paramount necessity for the writ to prevent serious damage.
suggestedAnswer.application: The patent owner admitted in its complaint the dates of issuance and of expiry, so the expiry needs no further evidence, and there is no showing of palpable mistake. After that date it no longer had the exclusive right to make, use and sell the patented articles. When the appellate court issued the restraining order, the first requisite, a clear right to be protected, was missing. Since the patent that was the basis of the injunction was no longer valid, the question of extending an injunction became moot and academic, and the case should have been dismissed.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The restraining order was improper, and the petition that sought to extend the injunction should have been dismissed as moot and academic.

keyPoints: The patentee's exclusive right to make, use and sell exists only during the term of the patent (Section 37, R.A. No. 165; seventeen years under Section 21)
An admission in the same case needs no proof unless made through palpable mistake or never made (Section 4, Rule 129)
Injunctive relief needs a clear and unmistakable right to be protected and an urgent and paramount necessity to prevent serious damage
After the patent expired there was no right to protect, so the restraining order was improper
The issue of extending the injunction was moot and academic once the patent was no longer valid

source.caseTitle: Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc. and Pfizer (Phil.) Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the first issue (injunction after the patent has lapsed)
source.excerpt: It is clear from the above-quoted provision of law that the exclusive right of a patentee to make, use and sell a patented product, article or process exists only during the term of the patent. … On the basis of the foregoing, the Court agrees with petitioner that after July 16, 2004, respondents no longer possess the exclusive right to make, use and sell the articles or products covered by Philippine Letters Patent No. 21116. … From the foregoing, it can be inferred that two requisites must exist to warrant the issuance of an injunctive relief, namely: (1) the existence of a clear and unmistakable right that must be protected; and (2) an urgent and paramount necessity for the writ to prevent serious damage. In the instant case, it is clear that when the CA issued its January 18, 2005 Resolution approving the bond filed by respondents, the latter no longer had a right that must be protected, considering that Philippine Letters Patent No. 21116 which was issued to them already expired on July 16, 2004. Hence, the issuance by the CA of a temporary restraining order in favor of the respondents is not proper.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A company sues a competitor for patent infringement before an intellectual property agency, asking for damages and a permanent injunction. While that case is pending, the company files a second action against the same competitor in a regional trial court on the basis of a different patent for the same product, asking for the same kind of injunction and damages. The company argues that there can be no forum shopping because the two complaints rely on different patents. Is it right? What should happen to the second case? Explain, based on Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The company is guilty of forum shopping. A difference in the patents does not change the cause of action, because the rights violated, the acts complained of and the reliefs sought are the same. The second case should be dismissed.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: A cause of action is the act or omission by which a party violates a right of another (Section 2, Rule 2). Forum shopping exists where there is identity of parties, identity of the rights asserted and reliefs prayed for, founded on the same facts, and identity such that a judgment in one action would amount to res judicata in the other. What matters is the vexation caused to courts and litigants by a party who asks different courts or agencies to rule on the same or related causes or to grant substantially the same reliefs, creating a possibility of conflicting decisions. If forum shopping is not willful and deliberate, the subsequent case is dismissed without prejudice on the ground of litis pendentia or res judicata; if it is willful and deliberate, all the actions are dismissed with prejudice.
suggestedAnswer.application: In both complaints the company claimed an exclusive right to make, use and sell the same product and said the competitor violated it by importing, distributing and selling it. It asked for substantially the same restraining order, injunction, damages and forfeiture. That the patents were different is immaterial. A decision in one case would necessarily amount to res judicata in the other. If the company did not act willfully and deliberately, for example because it could believe that different patents allowed separate actions and it candidly told the second court of the pending case, then only the later case is dismissed, without prejudice, on the ground of litis pendentia.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The company committed forum shopping, and the second case should be dismissed on the ground of litis pendentia, without prejudice, unless the forum shopping was willful and deliberate, in which case both would be dismissed with prejudice.

keyPoints: A cause of action is the act or omission by which a party violates a right of another
The patents being different is immaterial if the rights violated, the acts and the reliefs are identical
Filing two apparently different actions with the same objective is forum shopping
A decision in one case would be res judicata in the other
If not willful and deliberate, the later case is dismissed without prejudice on litis pendentia or res judicata; if willful and deliberate, all actions are dismissed with prejudice

source.caseTitle: Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc. and Pfizer (Phil.) Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the third issue (forum shopping)
source.excerpt: Section 2, Rule 2 of the Rules of Court defines a cause of action as the act or omission by which a party violates a right of another. … Thus, it does not matter that the patents upon which the complaints were based are different. The fact remains that in both complaints the rights violated and the acts violative of such rights are identical. … Owing to the substantial identity of parties, reliefs and issues in the IPO and RTC cases, a decision in one case will necessarily amount to res judicata in the other action. It bears to reiterate that what is truly important to consider in determining whether forum shopping exists or not is the vexation caused the courts and parties-litigant by a party who asks different courts and/or administrative agencies to rule on the same or related causes and/or to grant the same or substantially the same reliefs, in the process creating the possibility of conflicting decisions being rendered by the different fora upon the same issue.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: The Bureau of Legal Affairs of the Intellectual Property Office issues a preliminary injunction in a patent infringement complaint but refuses to extend it. The patent owner challenges the refusal by a special civil action for certiorari in the Court of Appeals. The adverse party says that, under the Intellectual Property Code, only the Director General of the Intellectual Property Office can review the Bureau's rulings. Which tribunal has jurisdiction? Explain, based on Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The Court of Appeals has jurisdiction. The Director General reviews decisions of the Bureau, but the patent owner is challenging an interlocutory order, and for that there is no remedy within the agency, so certiorari under the Rules of Court in the Court of Appeals is proper.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 7(b) of Republic Act No. 8293, the Director General exercises exclusive appellate jurisdiction over decisions of the Director of the Bureau of Legal Affairs. But the Code is silent about any remedy against interlocutory orders of the Bureau, and the rules on administrative complaints for violations of intellectual property laws provide that interlocutory orders are not appealable. Where no remedy is prescribed within the administrative machinery, the Rules of Court apply suppletorily, so a special civil action for certiorari under Rule 65 is available when a party cannot appeal and has no other plain, speedy and adequate remedy. The doctrine of primary jurisdiction does not apply when the question is purely legal and will ultimately have to be decided by the courts.
suggestedAnswer.application: What the patent owner questions is not a decision but an interlocutory order denying the extension of a preliminary injunction. It cannot appeal that order and has no other plain, speedy and adequate remedy. Whether to extend the injunction is a purely legal question that does not need the agency's special knowledge of technical matters, and courts have the duty to determine whether there was grave abuse of discretion on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the government. The patent owner therefore correctly went to the Court of Appeals.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The Court of Appeals, not the Director General, has jurisdiction to review the Bureau's interlocutory order by certiorari.

keyPoints: Section 7(b) of R.A. No. 8293: the Director General has exclusive appellate jurisdiction over decisions of the Director of the Bureau of Legal Affairs
The Code is silent on remedies against interlocutory orders, and the IPO's rules say interlocutory orders are not appealable
In the absence of an agency remedy, the Rules of Court apply suppletorily, so certiorari under Rule 65 in the Court of Appeals is proper
An exception to primary jurisdiction is a purely legal question that will ultimately be decided by the courts
Courts decide whether any branch or instrumentality of government committed grave abuse of discretion

source.caseTitle: Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc. and Pfizer (Phil.) Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the second issue (which tribunal reviews interlocutory orders of the BLA-IPO)
source.excerpt: It is true that under Section 7(b) of RA 8293, otherwise known as the Intellectual Property Code of the Philippines, which is the presently prevailing law, the Director General of the IPO exercises exclusive appellate jurisdiction over all decisions rendered by the Director of the BLA-IPO. However, what is being questioned before the CA is not a decision, but an interlocutory order of the BLA-IPO denying respondents' motion to extend the life of the preliminary injunction issued in their favor. RA 8293 is silent with respect to any remedy available to litigants who intend to question an interlocutory order issued by the BLA-IPO. Moreover, Section 1(c), Rule 14 of the Rules and Regulations on Administrative Complaints for Violation of Laws Involving Intellectual Property Rights simply provides that interlocutory orders shall not be appealable. … Hence, in the absence of such a remedy, the provisions of the Rules of Court shall apply in a suppletory manner, as provided under Section 3, Rule 1 of the same Rules and Regulations. Hence, in the present case, respondents correctly resorted to the filing of a special civil action for certiorari with the CA to question the assailed Orders of the BLA-IPO, as they cannot appeal therefrom and they have no other plain, speedy and adequate remedy in the ordinary course of law.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In its complaint, a patent owner states the date its patent was issued and the date until which the patent is valid. Later, in the same case, the other party asks the court to require proof that the patent has expired on that date. According to Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc., how should the court treat the patent owner's statement?

choices.A: It is an admission that needs no proof and may be contradicted only by showing palpable mistake or that no such admission was made.
choices.B: It is only a claim and must be proved by evidence like any other fact.
choices.C: It binds only the patent owner in a different case, not in the same case.
choices.D: It can be freely withdrawn at any time before judgment.

questions.explanation: A is correct. The Court noted that the patent owners themselves admitted in their complaint the date of issuance and that the patent was valid until July 16, 2004, which accords with Section 21 of Republic Act No. 165 (a term of seventeen years from issuance). Under Section 4, Rule 129 of the Rules of Court, an admission made by a party in the course of the proceedings in the same case does not require proof, and it may be contradicted only by showing that it was made through palpable mistake or that no such admission was made. There was no such showing, so there was no need to present evidence of the expiry. B is wrong because admissions in the same case need no proof. C is wrong because the rule covers admissions in the same case. D is wrong because an admission can be contradicted only on the grounds stated.

source.caseTitle: Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc. and Pfizer (Phil.) Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the first issue (the term of the patent and the admission)
source.excerpt: They also admitted that the validity of the said patent is until July 16, 2004, which is in conformity with Section 21 of RA 165, providing that the term of a patent shall be seventeen (17) years from the date of issuance thereof. Section 4, Rule 129 of the Rules of Court provides that an admission, verbal or written, made by a party in the course of the proceedings in the same case, does not require proof and that the admission may be contradicted only by showing that it was made through palpable mistake or that no such admission was made.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: According to Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc., which of the following correctly states the elements of forum shopping?

choices.A: Only that the same party filed two cases in the same year.
choices.B: Only that both cases involve the same patent.
choices.C: (a) Identity of parties, or of parties representing the same interests; (b) identity of the rights asserted and reliefs prayed for, founded on the same facts; and (c) identity of the two preceding particulars such that a judgment in one action would amount to res judicata in the other.
choices.D: Only that a party lost in one forum and then filed an appeal in a higher court.

questions.explanation: C is correct. The decision lists these three elements. A and B state only one fact and are not the test; in this very case the two complaints relied on different patents, and the Court still found forum shopping because the rights violated, the acts and the reliefs were identical. D is wrong because forum shopping excludes seeking review by appeal or by the special civil action of certiorari; it is the seeking of another opinion in another forum, or the filing of two or more actions grounded on the same cause on the supposition that one or the other court would make a favorable disposition.

source.caseTitle: Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc. and Pfizer (Phil.) Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the third issue (the elements of forum shopping)
source.excerpt: The elements of forum shopping are: (a) identity of parties, or at least such parties that represent the same interests in both actions; (b) identity of rights asserted and reliefs prayed for, the reliefs being founded on the same facts; (c) identity of the two preceding particulars, such that any judgment rendered in the other action will, regardless of which party is successful, amount to res judicata in the action under consideration.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A court of appeals is asked to review a refusal to extend a preliminary injunction that was issued to protect a patent. While the appeal is pending, the patent lapses. According to Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc., what should the court do with the petition?

choices.A: Extend the injunction until the patent owner's damages claim is resolved.
choices.B: Remand the case to the intellectual property office for a fresh hearing.
choices.C: Convert the petition into an action for damages.
choices.D: Dismiss it, because with the patent no longer valid, the question of extending the injunction is moot and academic.

questions.explanation: D is correct. The Court said that the Court of Appeals should have granted the motion to dismiss the petition for certiorari, since the only issue raised was the propriety of extending the writ of preliminary injunction issued by the BLA-IPO. Because the patent that was the basis of the injunction was no longer valid, any issue about extending the life of the injunction was already rendered moot and academic. A is wrong because once the patent had lapsed, there was no right left to protect. B and C are not what the Court ordered; it dismissed the petition for certiorari for being moot and academic.

source.caseTitle: Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc. and Pfizer (Phil.) Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the first issue (mootness of the extension of the injunction)
source.excerpt: In fact, the CA should have granted petitioner's motion to dismiss the petition for certiorari filed before it as the only issue raised therein is the propriety of extending the writ of preliminary injunction issued by the BLA-IPO. Since the patent which was the basis for issuing the injunction, was no longer valid, any issue as to the propriety of extending the life of the injunction was already rendered moot and academic.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A party files two actions that amount to forum shopping, but the forum shopping is not willful and deliberate, and the party told the second court about the pending first case. According to Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc., what is the consequence?

choices.A: Both cases are dismissed with prejudice.
choices.B: The subsequent case is dismissed without prejudice, on the ground of litis pendentia or res judicata.
choices.C: The first case is dismissed, and the subsequent case continues.
choices.D: Neither case is dismissed, and the party only pays a fine.

questions.explanation: B is correct. The Court said that if forum shopping is not willful and deliberate, the subsequent case is dismissed without prejudice on the ground of either litis pendentia or res judicata, while if it is willful and deliberate, both (or all) actions are dismissed with prejudice. It found that Pfizer did not deliberately violate the rule, because it could erroneously believe that it could file separate actions on the basis of different patents, and because it candidly told the trial court of the pending complaint and petition. So only the Makati civil case was dismissed, on the ground of litis pendentia. A describes the consequence of willful and deliberate forum shopping. C and D are not what the Court held.

source.caseTitle: Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc. and Pfizer (Phil.) Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the third issue (consequence of forum shopping)
source.excerpt: Jurisprudence holds that if the forum shopping is not considered willful and deliberate, the subsequent case shall be dismissed without prejudice, on the ground of either litis pendentia or res judicata. However, if the forum shopping is willful and deliberate, both (or all, if there are more than two) actions shall be dismissed with prejudice. In the present case, the Court finds that respondents did not deliberately violate the rule on non-forum shopping. Respondents may not be totally blamed for erroneously believing that they can file separate actions simply on the basis of different patents. Moreover, in the suit filed with the RTC of Makati City, respondents were candid enough to inform the trial court of the pendency of the complaint filed with the BLA-IPO as well as the petition for certiorari filed with the CA. On these bases, only Civil Case No. 04-754 should be dismissed on the ground of litis pendentia.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A patent owner files its infringement complaint with the intellectual property office instead of a regular court. The defendant argues that this was wrong. According to Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc., why was filing the complaint with the intellectual property office first proper?

choices.A: Because the doctrine of primary jurisdiction applies: deciding whether the defendant violated the patent rights requires the agency's sound administrative discretion, based on its special competence, knowledge and experience.
choices.B: Because regular courts have no jurisdiction over patent matters of any kind.
choices.C: Because the defendant had agreed in advance to file there.
choices.D: Because the agency's decisions are never subject to review by any court.

questions.explanation: A is correct. The Court said that in specialized disputes the practice is to refer them to an administrative agency of special competence under the doctrine of primary jurisdiction, and it found that the initial filing with the BLA-IPO was in keeping with that doctrine because determining whether the petitioner violated the respondents' patent rights requires the exercise by the IPO of sound administrative discretion based on the agency's special competence, knowledge and experience. B is wrong because the doctrine applies where the claim is originally cognizable in the courts but its enforcement requires resolving issues placed within the special competence of an administrative body, in which case the court suspends its process and refers those issues to the agency. C has no basis in the decision. D is wrong because the Court itself reviewed the matter, and the Court of Appeals could review the interlocutory order by certiorari.

source.caseTitle: Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc. and Pfizer (Phil.) Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the second issue (the doctrine of primary jurisdiction)
source.excerpt: Based on the foregoing, the Court finds that respondents' initial filing of their complaint with the BLA-IPO, instead of the regular courts, is in keeping with the doctrine of primary jurisdiction owing to the fact that the determination of the basic issue of whether petitioner violated respondents' patent rights requires the exercise by the IPO of sound administrative discretion which is based on the agency's special competence, knowledge and experience.
